readerTitle: The supplier calls on Saturday: what do you do before you know?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 식료품점, 금속 부품 공장) + 실제 연구 (위기 정보 선제 공개 효과, 위기 커뮤니케이션 이론)
insight: 위기에서 확실해질 때까지 기다리는 것은 신중함이 아니라 피해를 키우는 선택일 수 있다. 아는 만큼 먼저 막고, 먼저 알린다.
misconception: 사실을 다 확인하기 전에는 아무 말도 하지 않는 것이 안전하다. 조용히 처리하면 평판을 지킬 수 있다.

sources.text: Arpan, L. M., & Roskos-Ewoldsen, D. R. (2005). Stealing thunder: Analysis of the effects of proactive disclosure of crisis information. Public Relations Review, 31(3).
Coombs, W. T. (2007). Protecting organization reputations during a crisis: The development and application of situational crisis communication theory. Corporate Reputation Review, 10(3).
식료품점과 부품 공장 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Arpan & Roskos-Ewoldsen(2005)의 결론(조직이 스스로 위기를 먼저 공개하면 제3자가 보도할 때보다 신뢰도가 높게 평가됨)을 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 수치 없이 방향만 적었습니다.
Coombs(2007) SCCT의 '피해자가 스스로를 보호할 정보(instructing information)를 평판 관리보다 먼저 제공하라'는 요지를 원문으로 확인하세요.
식료품점(샐러드 약 30봉지)과 브래킷 공장(고객사 3곳, 원인 조사 약 1주) 수치는 모두 가상입니다. 리콜·신고 의무는 국가·업종별로 달라 구체적 법률 조언은 하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Saturday, 8:40 a.m. The supplier calls.
body: You manage a neighborhood grocery store. Your bagged-salad supplier says one batch *may* be contaminated. Lab results arrive Monday.
About 30 bags from that batch sit on your shelves. Some sold yesterday. You don't know yet if anything is wrong. You have to decide anyway.

image.label: Store manager on the phone beside a shelf of salad bags
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 이른 아침 동네 식료품점, 매니저가 휴대폰을 귀에 대고 샐러드 봉지 진열대 앞에 서 있음. 벽시계는 8:40. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What do you do first?
body: The supplier can't confirm anything until Monday. It's your busiest weekend of the month.

options.text: Pull the batch, post a notice at the door and online, and tell buyers what you know so far
options.feedback: You lose some sales and admit a problem that may turn out to be nothing. In return, anyone at risk can act now, and customers hear it from you first.

options.text: Pull the batch quietly and wait for Monday's results before saying anything
options.feedback: This stops new harm from the shelf. But people who already bought a bag can't protect themselves, and if it comes out later, the silence becomes the story.

options.text: Leave it out until the lab confirms. A false alarm would scare customers
options.feedback: You avoid a possible false alarm, but you bet customers' health and your reputation on a test you haven't seen.

cards.title: The same bad news, two different stories.
body: Say Monday's test comes back positive. The store that waited learns a customer got sick on Sunday. Now people aren't asking about the salad. They're asking **what you knew, and when**.
The store that spoke on Saturday gets the same result. But its story is "the shop that warned us early."
And if the test is negative? The early store loses a weekend of salad sales and sends one slightly awkward update. That's the whole cost.

cards.title: Crisis response
body: **Crisis response** is what you do in the first hours after something has gone wrong, before you have the full picture.
Its core rule: act on what you know now. Limit the harm first, tell the people affected second, find the cause after.
Waiting for certainty feels careful. In a crisis, the delay is often what does the damage.
cards.softwareNote: During an outage, a status update saying "We're seeing errors and investigating. Next update in 30 minutes" beats an hour of silence followed by a perfect explanation.

cards.title: Four moves for the first hour.

breakdown.label: Contain
breakdown.detail: Stop the harm spreading: pull stock, pause shipments

breakdown.label: Tell
breakdown.detail: Reach the people affected: what you know, what you don't

breakdown.label: Own
breakdown.detail: One person decides and one voice speaks

breakdown.label: Update
breakdown.detail: Say when you'll speak next, then keep that promise

cards.callout: Finding the cause comes after these, not before.
cards.softwareNote: Avoid starting with root cause analysis. Contain first, and then you can investigate.

cards.title: Telling it first earns trust.
body: In a 2005 study, Laura Arpan and David Roskos-Ewoldsen showed people news of an organization's crisis. When the organization disclosed the problem itself, readers judged it **more credible** than when the same news came from someone else.

Crisis researcher W. Timothy Coombs makes a related point. First give people the information they need to protect themselves. Only then work on your reputation. Done in that order, the first step usually helps the second.

cards.title: Speed is not the same as guessing.
body: Say what you know, not what you hope. Naming a cause or blaming a supplier too early can force a correction, and corrections cost more trust than "we don't know yet."
Don't promise "this will never happen again" on day one.
Rules on recalls and reporting differ by country and industry. Learn yours before a crisis, not during one.

cards.title: Now it's a parts factory.
body: You make steel brackets. On Wednesday, a quality check finds a heat-treatment furnace ran too cool for part of last week. Brackets from those lots may be weaker than spec.
They've shipped to three customers. A full review of the cause will take about a week.

image.label: Factory floor with flagged pallets of brackets
image.brief: 금속 부품 공장 출하장. 브래킷이 담긴 팔레트 세 개에 빨간 'HOLD' 태그와 로트 번호 라벨. 뒤편에 열처리로. 실제 기업 로고는 쓰지 않음.

options.text: Call the three customers today with the lot numbers, ask them to hold those parts, and offer replacements
options.feedback: You admit a mistake before you fully understand it. In return, weak parts stop moving down the line, and customers trust what you tell them next.

options.text: Finish the week-long review first so you can give customers a complete answer
options.feedback: A full answer is valuable, but for a week the suspect brackets keep going into customers' products. Call now and send the review when it's done.

options.text: Ship replacements with the next regular order and swap the parts quietly
options.feedback: It avoids an awkward call, but customers may install the weak parts before the swap. If they find out later, they'll question every lot you ship.

cards.title: In a crisis, act on what you know now.
body: Contain the harm, tell the people affected, name one owner, and promise the next update. The full answer can follow.
**Try it today:** if your most important product had to be pulled tomorrow, who would decide, who would speak, and how would you reach customers who already bought it? Write down all three.
